newsitem.title: BULGARIA: BULGARIA ELECTION MEANINGLESS FOR GHETTO-DWELLERS.
newsitem.headline: BULGARIA ELECTION MEANINGLESS FOR GHETTO-DWELLERS.

text.p: The Gypsies and ethnic Turks who live in the notorious Stolipinovo ghetto in Bulgaria's second city hold out little hope of change after Saturday's elections.
They say they have seen too many politicians promise them the earth then leave them to their poverty until campaign time comes round again.
About 50,000 Gypsies and ethnic Bulgarian Turks, some crammed 20 to a room, live in run-down apartment blocks in the Stolipinovo quarter of Plovdiv, 150 km (90 miles) southeast of the capital Sofia.
"I can't see any difference between the parties. Maybe there is some but in their policy towards us they have all been the same -- they all neglected us," said carpenter Nikola Vatsev, 45.
Some 500 people gathered on Wednesday despite the rain for a folk concert organised by the Union for National Salvation, a coalition which includes the ethnic Turks' Movement for Rights and Freedoms.
"We have seen this many times before -- party leaders come with musicians ahead of the elections, then they desert us," said Simeon Iliev, who has lived all his 32 years in Stolipinovo.
Anton Karagyozov, chairman of Bulgaria's Roma foundation, said most Stolipinovo inhabitants were unemployed and relied on welfare benefits, which he said had not been paid for months.
"How can we make a living when we are the first to be laid off every time there are cuts in the factories," said Ivo Ivanov.
Bulgaria's 300,000 Gypsies are thought to have first come to Europe from the Punjab region of India around the 10th century.

In the 19th century they were mainly craftsmen -- basketmakers, combmakers, blacksmiths and tinkers -- but the emergence of manufacturing industry at the turn of the century limited the scope of their activities.

They were nomadic until the 1960s, when the communist government began a campaign of assimilation, severely curbing their religious and cultural traditions and forcing them to settle in Soviet-style collective farms or in housing projects.

After the collapse of communism in 1989 they lost access to jobs previously reserved for them and many of their welfare benefits. More then 70 percent are believed to be jobless and the same number are thought to be illiterate.
Some Gypsies scratch a living by collecting waste paper and bottles for recycling. Others turn to crime.

Residents of Stolipinovo, already at the bottom of the social heap, have been hard hit by the economic crash of the past few months. Prices of basic goods have soared as the national currency collapsed.
"We are starving to death, it is better for me to die than to watch my three children starve," said single mother Natalia Atanasova, adding that she would not vote on Saturday.

More than 300,000 ethnic Turks joined an exodus to Turkey in 1989, at the height of an assimilation campaign by the former communist rulers which forced them to change their Turkish names for Slavic ones. Many have since returned and ethnic Turks account for about 10 percent of the population.

The Union of Democratic Forces, the favourite to win the election, has also pledged social welfare programmes for minorities but they are unlikely to be a high priority for a government struggling to stabilise the economy.
With even relatively well-off Bulgarians facing more hardship as the government implements tough economic reforms, the outlook for Stolipinovo looks grim.

"There have been so many governments since the collapse of one-party rule in 1989 and nothing has changed here," said Dragan Manolov, 58. "We have been deceived so many times, how can we believe them now?"
